title: Finance and Business
objectives: Làm matching features: nối luận điểm (paraphrase) với đúng nhà nghiên cứu
Trả lời global multiple choice: mục đích và thái độ của toàn bài
Viết Task 2 agree/disagree với lập trường nhất quán và nhượng bộ có kiểm soát
Dùng modal và cụm thận trọng để nói về khả năng (may well, is likely to, arguably)
exam_strategy: Matching features: một người có thể xuất hiện ở nhiều đoạn; gom mọi ý của từng người trước khi trả lời. Câu hỏi diễn đạt lại ý tưởng – đừng tìm từ trùng.
core_outcome: Phân tích các quan điểm khác nhau về thành công kinh doanh; viết Task 2 nhất quán và thừa nhận phản biện hợp lý.

grammar.title: Degrees of certainty and speculation
grammar.explanation_vi: Band 6–7 cần thể hiện mức độ chắc chắn tinh tế: will/is certain to (chắc chắn) → is likely to / may well (khá có khả năng) → may/might/could (có thể) → is unlikely to (ít khả năng). Với quá khứ: must have / may have / can't have + V3. Arguably và to some extent giúp nêu nhận định có chừng mực.
grammar.form: S + will / is likely to / may well / might / is unlikely to + V · It is (highly) likely / unlikely that … · S + must have / may have / can't have + V3 · Arguably, … · to some extent
examples: Interest rates are likely to remain high for at least another year.
The company may well lose customers if it raises its prices again.
The firm can't have expected such a sharp fall in demand.
examples_vi: Lãi suất có khả năng sẽ vẫn ở mức cao ít nhất thêm một năm.
Công ty rất có thể sẽ mất khách nếu lại tăng giá.
Công ty hẳn đã không lường trước được sự sụt giảm nhu cầu mạnh như vậy.
grammar.trap: must have + V3 = chắc chắn đã (suy luận về quá khứ), không phải nghĩa vụ. can't have + V3 = chắc chắn đã không. Không viết “may well to” (đúng: may well + V).
items: Prices are ___ to rise next year, according to most economists. (likely / probably)
likely
be likely to + V; probably là trạng từ, không đi với to.
The shop may ___ close if sales do not improve. (một từ tăng mức khả năng)
well
may well + V = rất có thể.
Profits fell sharply, so the strategy ___ have worked. (must not / can't)
can't
can't have + V3 = chắc chắn đã không.
The office is empty; everyone ___ have gone home. (must / should)
must
must have + V3 = suy luận chắc chắn về quá khứ.
It is highly ___ that the merger will be approved; regulators have strong objections. (likely / unlikely)
unlikely
Ngữ cảnh phản đối mạnh → ít khả năng.
___, the new tax helped small firms more than large ones. (một trạng từ nêu nhận định có thể tranh luận)
Arguably
Arguably = có thể cho rằng.
To some ___, the bank was responsible for the losses.
extent
to some extent = ở mức độ nào đó.
Correct the error: The company may well to expand into Asia.
The company may well expand into Asia.
may well + V nguyên mẫu, không có to.

readings.title: What makes a business successful?
readings.strategy: Matching features: gạch dưới tên 5 nhà nghiên cứu; mỗi lần gặp tên, ghi chú ý chính của người đó bên lề. Câu hỏi global: chọn phương án bao quát toàn bài, loại phương án chỉ đúng một đoạn.
readings.instruction_vi: Bài đọc khoảng 850 từ, 13 câu: 7 câu nối ý kiến với người nói (A–E), 3 câu global multiple choice và 3 câu short-answer.
paragraphs: A

Ask a hundred business leaders how they measure success and most will mention profit. Profit is easy to calculate, easy to compare between companies and, for publicly listed firms, closely watched by investors. Yet in recent decades a growing number of economists and management researchers have argued that profit alone gives an incomplete, and sometimes misleading, picture of how well a business is performing. Their criticisms vary considerably, however, and the alternatives they propose are not always compatible with one another.
B

The most traditional defence of profit comes from economist Martin Hale, who argues that profit is the best available signal that a company is using resources efficiently. If a firm can sell its products for more than they cost to make, he reasons, it must be creating something that customers value. Hale accepts that some companies make profits in harmful ways, but he believes this is a problem for regulators rather than a reason to abandon profit as a measure. In his view, asking managers to pursue several goals at once simply makes them less accountable.
C

Professor Leila Nasser, who studies corporate governance, takes a different view. She points out that profit is calculated over short periods – usually a quarter or a year – and that managers under pressure to report rising profits may cut spending on research, training or maintenance, which damages the company's long-term prospects. In her research on two hundred manufacturing firms, those that reported the most consistent short-term profit growth were also the most likely to have reduced their investment in new equipment. Nasser does not reject profit, but she argues it should be judged over five or ten years rather than one.
D

A third perspective focuses on stakeholders – employees, customers, suppliers and local communities, as well as shareholders. Business ethicist Daniel Osei argues that a company which treats its workers badly or misleads its customers may be profitable for a while, but is building up risks that will eventually surface, for example in strikes, lawsuits or a loss of reputation. Osei has proposed a balanced scorecard that measures staff turnover, customer complaints and supplier relationships alongside financial results. Critics note that such scorecards can become so complicated that it is unclear which measure should take priority when they conflict.
E

Economist Rosa Lindgren is sceptical of what she calls 'measurement inflation'. Every new indicator, she argues, creates new opportunities for managers to present their performance favourably. If a company is rewarded for reducing customer complaints, for instance, it may make complaining more difficult rather than improving its service. Lindgren's own research suggests that a small number of carefully chosen measures, regularly reviewed, works better than a long list. She also emphasises that numbers should always be checked against the judgement of people who know the business well.
F

The debate has taken on new urgency because of environmental concerns. Many companies now publish reports on their carbon emissions and water use. Supporters see this as progress; sceptics point out that the figures are often unaudited and that firms choose which activities to include. Finance researcher Hiroshi Tanaka has found that companies with the most detailed environmental reports do not necessarily have the lowest emissions. Some appear to use detailed reporting as a substitute for real change, a practice he describes as 'disclosure without improvement'.
G

Despite their disagreements, these researchers share one important conclusion: no single number can capture everything that matters about a business. Even Hale concedes that profit should be interpreted alongside other information, such as the company's debts and the risks it is taking. The real question, then, is not whether to use profit but how to combine it with other evidence in a way that is transparent and difficult to manipulate.
H

For smaller businesses, these debates can seem remote. A family-owned shop or a new technology start-up is unlikely to produce a balanced scorecard or an environmental report. Yet the underlying questions are the same. Is the business serving its customers well? Can it keep its best employees? Will it still be viable in ten years? Owners who ask these questions regularly, researchers suggest, are more likely to survive difficult periods than those who look only at this year's figures.
I

The measurement of business success is therefore less a technical problem than a question of values. Deciding what to measure means deciding what a business is for, and that is a question on which reasonable people are likely to continue to disagree. What the research does make clear is that the choice of measure shapes behaviour, so it deserves at least as much attention as the results themselves.

questions.prompt: Profit shows that a company is using its resources efficiently.
questions.why: Đoạn B: Hale cho rằng lợi nhuận là tín hiệu sử dụng nguồn lực hiệu quả.

questions.prompt: Pressure for short-term results may lead managers to cut long-term investment.
questions.why: Đoạn C: quản lý cắt chi nghiên cứu, đào tạo, bảo trì để báo lợi nhuận tăng.

questions.prompt: Adding more performance indicators can encourage managers to present results misleadingly.
questions.why: Đoạn E: “measurement inflation” – mỗi chỉ số mới tạo cơ hội trình bày có lợi.

questions.prompt: Harmful ways of making profit should be dealt with by regulators.
questions.why: Đoạn B: “a problem for regulators rather than a reason to abandon profit”.

questions.prompt: Detailed reporting can sometimes replace genuine change.
questions.why: Đoạn F: “disclosure without improvement”.

questions.prompt: Treating staff or customers badly creates risks that will appear later.
questions.why: Đoạn D: rủi ro sẽ bộc lộ qua đình công, kiện tụng, mất uy tín.

questions.prompt: Numbers should be checked against the views of people who know the business.
questions.why: Đoạn E: “numbers should always be checked against the judgement of people who know the business well”.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: A. To prove that profit is a useless measure
B. To compare different views on how business success should be measured
C. To explain how to calculate profit
D. To recommend environmental reporting for all firms
questions.answer: B. To compare different views on how business success should be measured
questions.why: Cả bài trình bày quan điểm của năm nhà nghiên cứu và điểm chung của họ.

questions.prompt: What do all the researchers agree on?
options: B. Balanced scorecards are the best method.
C. No single number can capture everything important.
D. Small businesses need environmental reports.
questions.answer: C. No single number can capture everything important.
questions.why: Đoạn G: “no single number can capture everything that matters”.

questions.prompt: How does the writer describe the measurement of business success in the final paragraph?
options: A. As mainly a technical calculation
B. As a question of values
D. As irrelevant to small firms
questions.answer: B. As a question of values
questions.why: Đoạn I: “less a technical problem than a question of values”.

questions.prompt: How many manufacturing firms did Nasser study? Write A NUMBER.
questions.why: Đoạn C: “two hundred manufacturing firms”.

questions.prompt: What does Osei call his proposed measurement tool? Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS.
questions.why: Đoạn D: “a balanced scorecard”.

questions.prompt: Over how many years does Nasser think profit should be judged? Write NO MORE THAN FOUR WORDS.
questions.why: Đoạn C: “over five or ten years rather than one”.

readings.title: Should money be taught at school?
readings.strategy: Matching features với các nhóm (giáo viên, phụ huynh, nhà nghiên cứu): đáp án dựa trên ý kiến, không phải chủ đề nhóm đó được nhắc tới.
paragraphs: A

Surveys in many countries show that a large proportion of adults struggle with basic financial decisions, such as comparing loan offers or understanding how interest builds up on credit card debt. In response, a growing number of governments have added financial literacy to the school curriculum. Students learn how to make a budget, how to save and how to recognise common scams. Whether these lessons actually change behaviour in adult life, however, is still being debated.
B

Teachers are generally supportive but cautious. Many report that students find the topic engaging, especially when lessons involve realistic situations such as planning a first month living away from home. However, teachers also point out that financial education is often squeezed into a few hours a year, usually taught by staff with no specialist training. Without more time and support, they argue, it is unrealistic to expect lasting effects.
C

Researchers are divided. A large review of studies published by the fictional Centre for Economic Learning found that short courses had only small effects on behaviour, and that these often faded within two years. Other researchers argue that the review included many poorly designed programmes, and that well-designed courses, especially those delivered close to a real decision such as opening a first bank account, can have more lasting effects.
D

Parents, meanwhile, play a role that schools cannot easily replace. Studies of young adults consistently find that those whose parents discussed money openly at home are more likely to save regularly and less likely to fall into debt. Some education experts therefore suggest that schools should involve families, for example by setting tasks that students complete with parents, rather than treating financial education as a purely classroom subject.
E

There is also a more critical argument. Some economists warn that focusing on individual financial skills may distract from the responsibility of banks and lenders. If financial products are deliberately complicated, they argue, the solution is better regulation and clearer pricing, not simply asking teenagers to read the small print more carefully. Supporters of financial education reply that both approaches are needed, since regulation cannot protect people from every poor decision.
F

What seems clear is that financial literacy is not a single skill learned once. Like other forms of literacy, it develops gradually and needs to be practised in real situations. Schools can lay a foundation, but they are only one part of a wider system that includes families, employers and financial institutions. Programmes that recognise this, and connect classroom lessons with real decisions students face, appear to have the best chance of lasting success.

questions.prompt: Financial lessons are often too short and taught by non-specialists.
options: B. The Centre for Economic Learning
questions.why: Đoạn B: giáo viên nói môn học bị dồn vào vài giờ, dạy bởi người không chuyên.

questions.prompt: Short courses have small effects that often fade.
options: B. The Centre for Economic Learning
questions.answer: B. The Centre for Economic Learning
questions.why: Đoạn C: tổng quan của Centre for Economic Learning.

questions.prompt: Better regulation of financial products is needed.
options: B. The Centre for Economic Learning
questions.why: Đoạn E: “the solution is better regulation and clearer pricing”.

questions.prompt: Schools should involve families in financial education.
options: B. The Centre for Economic Learning
questions.why: Đoạn D: “Some education experts therefore suggest that schools should involve families”.

questions.prompt: Students usually find financial lessons boring.
questions.why: Đoạn B: “students find the topic engaging”.

questions.prompt: Some researchers believe the review included poorly designed programmes.
questions.why: Đoạn C: “the review included many poorly designed programmes”.

questions.prompt: Young adults whose parents discussed money are less likely to fall into debt.
questions.why: Đoạn D: “less likely to fall into debt”.

questions.prompt: Banks have opposed the introduction of financial education in schools.
questions.why: Bài không nói ngân hàng phản đối.

questions.prompt: The writer believes schools alone can make young people financially literate.
questions.why: Đoạn F: trường học “only one part of a wider system”.

readings.title: Buy now, pay later
readings.strategy: Global multiple choice: đọc câu đầu mỗi đoạn để nắm cấu trúc lập luận; câu hỏi về thái độ người viết thường nằm ở đoạn cuối.
paragraphs: A

In the space of a few years, 'buy now, pay later' services have become a familiar option at online checkouts. Instead of paying the full price immediately, customers can split a purchase into several interest-free instalments, usually paid over six to eight weeks. The services are free for customers who pay on time; providers earn most of their income from fees charged to retailers, who are willing to pay because the option tends to increase sales.
B

For many customers, the appeal is obvious. Spreading the cost of a large purchase makes it easier to manage a monthly budget, and unlike a credit card, there is no interest if payments are made on time. Younger shoppers in particular say they prefer these services because they feel more transparent than traditional credit. Some also value the fact that approval appears instantly at the checkout.
C

Consumer groups, however, have raised several concerns. Because approval is fast and often involves only a limited credit check, people may take on several arrangements at once without realising how much they owe in total. Late payment fees, while usually smaller than those on credit cards, can add up. Surveys in one fictional country found that around one in five users had missed at least one payment in the previous year.
D

A further concern is that these services may encourage people to spend more than they intended. Retailers report that customers using instalment payments tend to buy more items per order. Behavioural economists argue that splitting a price into smaller amounts makes it feel less significant, an effect that may be harmless for occasional purchases but risky for people who are already in financial difficulty.
E

Regulators in several countries are now considering new rules. Proposals include requiring providers to carry out proper affordability checks, making sure that late fees are clearly displayed before purchase, and sharing information with credit agencies so that other lenders can see how many arrangements a person has. Providers generally accept the need for some regulation but argue that strict rules could remove a useful, low-cost alternative to more expensive forms of credit.
F

The story of buy now, pay later illustrates a familiar pattern in finance: an innovation that offers genuine benefits to many users can also create risks for a vulnerable minority. The challenge for regulators is to protect that minority without removing the benefits for everyone else. How well different countries manage this balance is likely to become clearer over the next few years, as the first rules come into force and their effects can be measured.

questions.prompt: How do 'buy now, pay later' providers earn most of their income?
options: A. From interest paid by customers
B. From fees charged to retailers
questions.answer: B. From fees charged to retailers
questions.why: Đoạn A: “earn most of their income from fees charged to retailers”.

questions.prompt: Why may people take on several arrangements at once?
options: A. Approval is fast with limited checks.
C. Interest rates are very high.
D. Credit cards are no longer available.
questions.answer: A. Approval is fast with limited checks.
questions.why: Đoạn C: “approval is fast and often involves only a limited credit check”.

questions.prompt: According to behavioural economists, why might splitting a price encourage spending?
options: A. It makes the price feel less significant.
B. It reduces the total cost.
C. It hides the name of the retailer.
D. It removes the need for a budget.
questions.answer: A. It makes the price feel less significant.
questions.why: Đoạn D: “makes it feel less significant”.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's overall view?
options: A. These services should be banned.
B. They are completely safe for all users.
C. They have real benefits but create risks for some users.
questions.answer: C. They have real benefits but create risks for some users.
questions.why: Đoạn F: lợi ích thật cho nhiều người nhưng rủi ro cho nhóm thiểu số dễ tổn thương.

questions.prompt: Over how long are instalments usually paid? Write NO MORE THAN FOUR WORDS.
questions.why: Đoạn A: “usually paid over six to eight weeks”.

questions.prompt: Which group of shoppers says these services feel more transparent? Write ONE WORD.
questions.why: Đoạn B: “Younger shoppers in particular”.

questions.prompt: What proportion of users in one survey had missed a payment? Write NO MORE THAN FOUR WORDS.
questions.why: Đoạn C: “around one in five users”.

questions.prompt: What do customers using instalments tend to buy more of per order? Write ONE WORD.
questions.why: Đoạn D: “tend to buy more items per order”.

questions.prompt: Name ONE proposed rule for providers. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS.
questions.why: Đoạn E: “proper affordability checks” – chấp nhận clearly displayed late fees.

listenings.title: Opening a business bank account
listenings.strategy: Short-answer: đọc giới hạn từ trong câu hỏi; tên công ty và mã số thường được đánh vần hoặc đọc từng chữ số.
listenings.pre_listening: Trước khi nghe: đoán mỗi câu cần tên, số hay khoảng thời gian.
listenings.trap: Phí hoặc thời gian thường được nói theo mức cũ trước rồi mới cập nhật.
listenings.transcript:
Adviser: Good morning, Northgate Bank business team. My name's Priya. How can I help?
Customer: Hello. I've just started a small business and I'd like to open a business account.
Adviser: Congratulations. What kind of business is it?
Customer: I make handmade ceramics – mostly tableware – and sell them online and at craft markets.
Adviser: Lovely. What's the name of the business?
Customer: It's called Clayborne Studio. That's C-L-A-Y-B-O-R-N-E.
Adviser: Thank you. Are you a sole trader, or have you registered a company?
Customer: A sole trader for now. I might register a company next year if it grows.
Adviser: That's fine. We have two accounts that might suit you. The Starter account has no monthly fee for the first eighteen months. After that, it's six pounds a month.
Customer: I read on your website that it was free for twelve months.
Adviser: That was the old offer – it was extended to eighteen months in January. The other option is the Trader account, which costs nine pounds a month but includes card payments at markets with a lower fee per transaction.
Customer: How much lower?
Adviser: On the Starter account, card payments cost one point nine per cent. On the Trader account, it's one point two per cent.
Customer: I think I'll start with the Starter account and switch later if market sales increase.
Adviser: Sensible. You can switch at any time without a charge. To open the account, I'll need photo identification and proof of your home address, such as a recent council tax bill.
Customer: No problem. How long does it take?
Adviser: Once we have your documents, the account is usually open within five working days. You'll receive your card by post about a week later.
Customer: And is there any support for new businesses?
Adviser: Yes, we offer a free online course on bookkeeping, and you can book a session with a business adviser. The first session is free.
Customer: That sounds useful. Thank you.

questions.prompt: What does the customer mainly make?
questions.why: “handmade ceramics – mostly tableware”.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the business? (one word + Studio)
questions.why: Đánh vần C-L-A-Y-B-O-R-N-E.

questions.prompt: What type of business is it at present? (TWO WORDS)
questions.why: “A sole trader for now.”

questions.prompt: For how many months is the Starter account free?
questions.why: 12 tháng là ưu đãi cũ (bẫy); nay 18 tháng.

questions.prompt: What is the Starter account's monthly fee after that? (£)
questions.why: “it's six pounds a month”.

questions.prompt: What percentage is charged per card payment on the Trader account?
questions.why: Starter 1,9%; Trader 1,2%.

questions.prompt: What document is suggested as proof of address? (THREE WORDS)
questions.why: “a recent council tax bill”.

questions.prompt: How many working days does opening the account usually take?
questions.why: “within five working days”.

questions.prompt: What subject is the free online course about?
questions.why: “a free online course on bookkeeping”.

listenings.title: Inside a coffee roastery
listenings.strategy: Diagram labelling: theo dõi các bước theo thứ tự người nói đi qua; tên máy và công đoạn là danh từ ngắn.
listenings.transcript:
Guide: Welcome to Hillside Coffee Roasters. Today I'll take you through the journey our coffee makes, from the sacks of green beans you see behind me to the bags on supermarket shelves. I'll explain each stage of the diagram on the wall as we go.
Everything starts here, in the receiving area. Green coffee beans arrive in jute sacks, usually weighing sixty kilograms each, from farms in five countries. Before anything else happens, a sample from each sack is tested in our small laboratory to check the moisture content. If the beans are too wet, they can't be roasted evenly.
Next, the beans go into the cleaning machine, which removes stones, twigs and other material. You'd be surprised how much we find.
The third stage, and the most important, is the roaster itself – the large drum you can see in the centre of the room. The beans are heated to around two hundred degrees, and the roaster operator decides exactly when to stop. A few seconds too long can make the coffee taste bitter.
As soon as roasting finishes, the hot beans fall into the cooling tray, where a fan and rotating arms bring their temperature down within about four minutes. If they stayed hot, they would continue to cook.
After cooling, the beans rest in storage silos for at least twelve hours. This allows gases produced during roasting to escape. Some customers want ground coffee, so part of each batch goes through the grinder at this point.
Finally, the coffee is packed. Our bags have a one-way valve, which lets remaining gas out without letting air in, so the coffee stays fresh for longer.
The whole process, from green beans to sealed bag, takes about a day and a half. Any questions before we move on to the tasting room?

questions.prompt: Stage 1 – receiving: sacks usually weigh ______ kg
questions.why: “weighing sixty kilograms each”.

questions.prompt: Stage 1 – samples are tested for ______ content
questions.why: “to check the moisture content”.

questions.prompt: Stage 2 – the ______ machine removes stones and twigs
questions.why: “the cleaning machine, which removes stones, twigs”.

questions.prompt: Stage 3 – beans heated to about ______ °C
questions.why: “heated to around two hundred degrees”.

questions.prompt: Stage 3 – roasting too long makes coffee taste ______
questions.why: “can make the coffee taste bitter”.

questions.prompt: Stage 4 – cooling takes about ______ minutes
questions.why: “within about four minutes”.

questions.prompt: Stage 5 – beans rest in storage ______
questions.why: “rest in storage silos”.

questions.prompt: Stage 5 – minimum resting time: ______ hours
questions.why: “for at least twelve hours”.

questions.prompt: Stage 6 – bags have a one-way ______
questions.why: “a one-way valve”.

listenings.title: Discussing a business case study
listenings.strategy: Hai sinh viên phân tích tình huống doanh nghiệp: phân biệt ý kiến ban đầu và kết luận cuối cùng của họ.
listenings.transcript:
Tutor: So, Ben and Hana, what did you make of the Greenleaf case study?
Ben: Well, Greenleaf is a regional supermarket chain that decided to stop competing on price with the big national chains. Instead, it focused on local produce and customer service.
Hana: At first, I thought it was a risky decision. Their sales actually fell by about eight per cent in the first year.
Ben: But the profit margin went up, because local products could be sold at higher prices and there was less waste.
Tutor: So was it a success?
Hana: I think we need to look further. By the third year, sales had recovered and were higher than before the change. And staff turnover had halved, which saved a lot on recruitment and training.
Ben: Although we should be careful. The case study says that two of their main competitors closed stores in the region during the same period, so some of that recovery might be because customers had fewer alternatives.
Tutor: Good point. That's a classic problem when evaluating a strategy. What would you need to know to be more confident?
Hana: Ideally, we'd compare towns where competitors closed with towns where they didn't. If Greenleaf did well in both, the strategy is more likely to be the reason.
Ben: The case study doesn't give that data, unfortunately.
Tutor: So what will your conclusion be?
Hana: That the strategy seems to have improved profitability and staff retention, but we can't be sure how much of the sales recovery was caused by the strategy itself.
Ben: And we'll recommend that Greenleaf collects data by town in future, so it can evaluate decisions like this more reliably.
Tutor: Excellent. Make sure your report separates what the evidence shows from what you're inferring. And remember the word limit – three thousand words, not including the appendix with the financial tables.
Hana: Should we include the interviews with store managers in the appendix as well?
Tutor: Yes, summaries are fine there. Quote them in the main text only when they support a specific point.

questions.prompt: What did Greenleaf decide to stop doing?
options: B. Competing on price with national chains
questions.answer: B. Competing on price with national chains
questions.why: “decided to stop competing on price with the big national chains”.

writing.instruction_vi: Đề “To what extent do you agree or disagree?”: nêu mức độ đồng ý ngay mở bài; mỗi thân bài một lý do ủng hộ lập trường; có một đoạn nhượng bộ ngắn và phản biện. Viết ít nhất 250 từ (mục tiêu 270–310).
writing.task: Some people believe that a cashless society, in which all payments are made electronically, would bring more benefits than drawbacks. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
writing.sample_answer:
In many countries, cash is rapidly being replaced by cards and mobile payments, and some people believe that eliminating cash altogether would be beneficial. While electronic payments offer clear advantages, I disagree that a completely cashless society would bring more benefits than drawbacks, because it would exclude vulnerable groups and increase certain risks.

It is true that electronic payments are convenient and efficient. Transactions are faster, businesses no longer need to handle and transport large amounts of money, and digital records make it much harder to hide income from tax authorities. In addition, card and mobile payments may reduce some kinds of crime, such as street robbery, because there is less cash to steal.

However, removing cash entirely would disadvantage people who are least able to adapt. Many older people, people with disabilities and those on very low incomes rely on cash because it is easy to understand and helps them control their spending. In rural areas with weak internet connections, electronic payments are also less reliable. A cashless society could therefore leave a significant minority unable to pay for everyday goods.

Furthermore, total reliance on electronic systems creates new vulnerabilities. A technical failure or cyberattack could prevent millions of people from buying food or paying for transport, and personal spending data could be misused by companies or governments. Cash, by contrast, works even when networks fail and does not record who bought what.

In conclusion, although electronic payments bring significant benefits and are likely to become even more widespread, I believe that a fully cashless society would create more problems than it solves. Governments should encourage digital payments while ensuring that cash remains available for those who need it.
guidance: Mở bài: paraphrase + lập trường rõ (disagree, với lý do định hướng).

Thân bài 2–3: hai lý do phản đối, mỗi lý do có cơ chế và ví dụ.
Kết luận: nhắc lại lập trường và đề xuất dung hòa.

essay.prompt: Some people think a company's success should be measured mainly by its profits. Others believe its treatment of employees, customers and the environment matters more. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
planning_prompts: Mở bài: hai quan điểm và ý kiến (lợi nhuận cần thiết nhưng không đủ).
Thân bài 1: lý do dùng lợi nhuận (rõ ràng, so sánh được, cho thấy giá trị với khách hàng).
Thân bài 2: lý do đánh giá rộng hơn (rủi ro dài hạn, nhân viên, môi trường).
Kết luận: kết hợp lợi nhuận dài hạn với vài chỉ số khác minh bạch.
model_paragraphs: There is ongoing debate about how the success of a company should be judged. Some argue that profit is the most reliable measure, while others believe that a firm's treatment of its staff, customers and the environment is more important. In my view, profit is necessary but not sufficient, and it should be assessed alongside a small number of other indicators.

Those who prioritise profit argue that it is a clear and objective measure. A company that consistently makes a profit is selling something customers are willing to pay for, and it is using its resources efficiently. Profit can also be compared easily between firms, which helps investors decide where to put their money. Without profits, a business cannot pay its workers, invest in new products or survive difficult periods.

On the other hand, critics point out that short-term profits can hide serious problems. A firm may cut training, delay maintenance or exploit suppliers to boost this year's results, damaging its long-term prospects. Companies that treat employees badly often suffer from high staff turnover, while those that harm the environment may face fines, lawsuits and loss of reputation. From this perspective, how a company makes its profit matters as much as how much it makes.

I believe the most sensible approach is to judge profit over several years rather than one, and to combine it with a few transparent measures such as staff turnover, customer satisfaction and verified emissions. Too many indicators, however, can make companies harder to hold accountable.

In conclusion, while profit remains an essential sign of a healthy business, it should not be the only measure of success. A balanced view that includes long-term performance and a company's impact on people and the environment gives a more accurate picture.

speaking.title: Money, shopping and business
speaking.instruction_vi: Part 3 về kinh tế: dùng mức độ chắc chắn (is likely to, may well) khi dự đoán; đưa ví dụ cụ thể từ Việt Nam.
speaking.focus: Dự đoán và suy đoán có mức độ (I'd say it's likely that…, it may well…) và phát âm rõ số liệu, phần trăm.
part1: Do you prefer paying by cash or by card?
Do you usually plan how you spend your money?
Did you learn about money when you were a child?
Would you like to run your own business one day?
speaking.part2: Describe a small business that you think is successful. You should say what the business is, who runs it, how you know about it, and explain why you think it is successful.
part3: Is profit the best measure of a business's success?
Should schools teach young people how to manage money?
How might online shopping change local businesses in the future?
speaking.model_answer: I'd like to talk about a small bookshop and café near my university that's run by a couple who used to work as teachers. I first went there about three years ago because a classmate recommended it as a quiet place to study, and I've been a regular customer ever since. From the outside it looks quite ordinary, but inside it's very cosy, with second-hand books on the walls and a few tables where students can sit for hours. I think it's successful for several reasons. First, the owners know exactly who their customers are. Most of them are students on a budget, so the drinks are reasonably priced, but they make money by selling books and by hosting small events like book clubs and English conversation evenings, which people pay a small fee to join. Second, they've built a real sense of community. They remember people's names and often recommend books based on what you've bought before. And third, they've adapted well. During the pandemic they started selling books online and delivering them by bicycle, and they've kept doing that because it was popular. So although it's not a big business, it seems to be very stable, and I think that's because it offers something that a large chain simply can't.

coaching.core: Đọc các chỉ số kinh tế và phân biệt doanh thu với hiệu quả thực
coaching.example: Company revenue rose 20%, but its costs rose faster. Higher revenue therefore does not guarantee higher profit.
coaching.trap: Diễn giải một chỉ số đơn lẻ thành thành công chung của doanh nghiệp.
coaching.reading_focus: Summary completion and arguments about business claims
coaching.listening_focus: Detecting budget revisions and changed forecasts
coaching.speaking_issue: Is profit the best measure of business success?

deep.grammar: Doanh thu (revenue) không đồng nghĩa lợi nhuận (profit). 'While revenue rose, operating costs grew faster' là hai thông tin cùng thời điểm nhưng đối lập kết quả. Dùng 'would depend on' khi quyết định còn chịu ảnh hưởng điều kiện. Tránh kết luận doanh nghiệp hiệu quả chỉ từ tăng trưởng bán hàng.
deep.reading: Summary completion cần kiểm tra loại từ, giới hạn số chữ và sự nhất quán ngữ pháp của câu có chỗ trống. Trước khi đọc, dự đoán chỗ trống cần danh từ chỉ kết quả hay yếu tố tác động. Sau đó tìm mệnh đề cùng nghĩa trong bài; từ khóa thường được diễn đạt lại nên không nhất thiết xuất hiện nguyên dạng.
deep.listening: Một buổi họp ngân sách thường có figures, alternatives và revisions. Khi nghe 'our forecast was £80,000, but the revised estimate is £95,000', ghi con số thứ hai. Đừng lẫn revenue, expenditure và profit. Trong Listening section 3, nhiều người nói có thể đồng ý một phần; quyết định cuối ở cuối đoạn mới quan trọng.
deep.writing: Opinion essay cần lập trường trả lời trực tiếp câu hỏi 'is profit the best measure?'. Một đoạn có thể nói profit đảm bảo tính bền vững; đoạn khác xét tác động lao động, chất lượng dịch vụ và uy tín dài hạn. Đừng dùng ví dụ tưởng tượng thành dữ kiện nghiên cứu đã công bố; đánh dấu giả định là 'for example, a local business might...'.
